title: Offline upgrade paths and network compatibility gates for Private/VPC deployments
creator: Sofia Patel
description: Define and validate requirements, acceptance gates, and test plans for performing safe upgrades of Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments where clusters have constrained network egress (partial or full air-gapped) and strict firewall rules. Deliver concrete preflight checks, network compatibility requirements, and rollback criteria for production rollouts.
background: Customers running Redwood Private have varied network topologies: fully isolated air-gapped datacenters, egress-restricted VPCs that allow only curated outbound endpoints (e.g., S3, internal artifact proxies), and hybrid networks with intermittent control-plane connectivity. Past upgrade attempts surfaced issues around image distribution, cert rotation, schema migrations, and operator health visibility when control-plane connectivity was limited.
goals: 1) Specify the minimum network surface and protocols required for both online and offline upgrade modes. 2) Define acceptance criteria and measurable gates for successful upgrades and rollbacks in air-gapped or egress-restricted environments. 3) Produce a reproducible test plan and runbooks for validating each step on customer-like topologies.
non_goals: 1) Rewriting the existing installer. 2) Implementing a brand new airgap bundle format in this ticket (this will be a follow-up). 3) Addressing unrelated private features such as RBAC UI changes.
requirements: A written matrix of allowed outbound endpoints (IP ranges and DNS names) and required ports for online upgrades.
A documented offline artifact bundle format and verification steps that can be consumed by the installer when there is zero outbound connectivity.
A preflight CLI that validates network egress, DNS resolution, certificate trust chains, disk free space, and operator health before attempting an upgrade.
Signed artifact verification: all upgrade bundles and images must be signed and verifiable offline using customer-supplied public keys or an integrated KMS/HSM.
Upgrade must support in-place and blue-green strategies per customer preference with clear rollback actions.
Clear rules for when automated DB or cache migrations are allowed vs requiring manual approval in air-gapped environments.
Observable upgrade state: controller must emit upgrade status events to local logs and optionally to the Redwood control plane when egress is available.
Detailed time-to-rollback objective: ability to fully revert an upgrade within 30 minutes for control-plane impacting incidents, with documented steps.
A network diagram template and instructions customers can use to produce a validated topology for Redwood support.
Acceptance test harnesses that can be run in CI and in an on-prem sandbox to validate networking and offline upgrade paths.
networking_requirements: Minimum egress endpoints for online upgrades: registry.redwood.ai (443), updates.redwood.ai (443), metrics.redwood.ai (443), s3.amazonaws.com (443) OR customer-provided artifact proxy endpoints.
Required ports: TCP 443 outbound for HTTPS endpoints; TCP 22 optional for SSH-based operator debugging (document as optional).
DNS requirements: cluster nodes must resolve above hostnames to configured proxies when required; support for no-DNS mode where customers provide /etc/hosts mappings in the preflight bundle.
Proxy support: installer must support HTTP(S) proxy env vars for image and bundle pulls and provide instructions to configure proxy credentials in air-gapped transfer steps.
Certificate and root trust: ability to install customer root CA so TLS validation works for internal registries and proxies.
Bandwidth guidance: provide recommended minimum bandwidth and concurrency settings for bulk image transfer in offline mode (e.g., 100 Mbps sustained for clusters >10 nodes).
airgap_constraints: Offline bundle must be consumable from local filesystem or local registry mirror; no runtime outbound connections required during install/upgrade when using bundle mode.
Bundle must include checksums and cryptographic signatures; installer will verify signatures against provided public keys before proceeding.
Bundle size and split rules: support splitting large bundles into sharded archives with checksums to accommodate restricted transport mechanisms (USB, internal artifact stores).
No-change policy: when operating in airgap/manual mode, automatic background migrations or external service calls must be disabled unless the operator explicitly enables them.
Metadata and manifest versioning: bundle manifest must include product version, component checksums, Kubernetes manifest revisions, and an upgrade ordering guide.
upgrade_strategy: Define three upgrade flows: 1) Online minimal-change (requires outbound egress), 2) Online proxied (uses customer artifact proxy/cache), 3) Offline bundle mode. Each flow includes preflight, dry-run validation, staged rollout (node-by-node or subset canary), and rollback plan. For Private deployments, prefer staged rollouts with health-checked probes and automatic abort on critical operator failures.
acceptance_criteria: Preflight checks pass in >90% of test sandboxes that replicate customer topologies (CI + on-prem workspace).
An upgrade executed in offline bundle mode completes end-to-end on a 5-node private cluster within documented time bounds and without requiring outbound connectivity.
Rollback from a failed upgrade restores previous cluster state and API responsiveness within 30 minutes, with no loss of application data persisted in Redwood-managed storage.
Signed bundle verification rejects tampered bundles (negative test) and accepts legitimate bundles signed with the provided keys.
Node-level continuous health probes show no sustained API error rate increase >1% and 99th percentile latency regresses by less than 20% post-upgrade for control-plane endpoints.
Upgrade process emits machine-readable logs and a post-upgrade summary artifact that includes component versions, migration actions performed, and checksums of applied bundles.
Customers can complete the documented runbook to perform an offline upgrade without Redwood support in at least two documented topologies (single-rack air-gapped and VPC with proxy).
testing_plan: Create CI scenarios that exercise online, proxied, and offline bundle upgrades against k8s test clusters with simulated firewall rules.
Run manual verification on an on-prem sandbox environment using large bundle sharding and USB transfer emulation.
Negative tests: corrupted bundle, missing signature, partial transfer; ensure installer fails safely and provides actionable diagnostics.
Performance tests: measure upgrade time and peak resource usage on clusters of size 3, 5, and 20 nodes and record regression metrics.
Run e2e validation that verifies post-upgrade API correctness, KV cache integrity, and operator reconciliation behavior.
Security tests: verify signature validation, artifact provenance, and KMS/HSM integration for signing keys.
rollout_plan: Phase 1: internal validation and CI (2 weeks). Phase 2: runbook + documentation review with two pilot customers (4 weeks). Phase 3: limited GA for Private customers with opt-in flag and 24/7 on-call coverage (6 weeks). Each phase includes automated and manual checkpoints and a go/no-go review with PM, Eng, Security, and Support.
notes_and_decisions: Decision: Offline bundle format will reuse existing artifact manifest with added signature fields to reduce engineering lift.
Decision: Support both customer KMS public keys and Redwood-managed signing for pilots; enterprise customers must provide their public key for high-security installs.
Trade-off: Sharded bundles increase installer complexity but are necessary for constrained transfer methods; we will first support single archive then iterate.
open_questions: Should we require manifests to include provenance metadata (build id, image digests) beyond checksums for traceability?
Do we need first-class support for non-HTTP image transfer protocols (e.g., OCI registry over TLS-internal-only) in this milestone?
What is the acceptable downtime window for customers during DB migrations in air-gapped upgrades (default vs. opt-in manual approval)?
